## Introduction

`depot` is a tool to catalog prospect[^1] datasets and make them discoverable across the Frontier

<!-- narrative -->

## Motivation

In modern research computing, accessing data is often a bottleneck. On
the one hand, an HPC cluster is simply a shared Linux file system with very little
guardrails and systems for data governance, and researchers technically
_can_ just move files around at their leisure. As a lab scales — both
in its workforce/user base, and its methods sophistication — this model quickly
devolves and leads to messy workspaces, poorly managed data, and an
increasing risk of irreproducibility. On the other hand, data governance
(such as that imposed by commercial data warehouse tools like AWS, Spark,
Databricks) can be overly strict, leading to workflows that incur several
days or weeks of bureaucracy just to do the simple task of accessing a file.

To maintain reproducibility and sufficient data governance while ensuring a 
speedy turnover of scientific assets, research computing needs a way to both
track data curation steps, but also provide quick access to data with the knowledge
that it may not yet be fully curated and certified. In industry, there are often
several "layers" of data in a data lakehouse, where raw data is considered
completely uncurated, while perfect data has been vetted, certified, tested,
documented, and published for access. In between these two extremes, there
can exist a squishy middle layer of data. To catalogue this middle layer,
we introduce `depot`, a tool for cataloging datasets that are in the process of being
curated, but are not yet fully certified for use in publications on the Frontier.

## Usage

### User Story

As research groups grow, datasets often become trapped inside individual 
projects and pipelines. Even when data exists and is technically 
accessible, other researchers may not know it exists, what transformations 
have been applied, or whether it is suitable for their work.

With `depot`, the researcher can query the catalog of developing 
datasets to find out the status of their data, and access it if it's available.

<!-- check the catalog -->

### API

## Internals

There have been several inventions across data science and software engineering
aimed at solving the problem of data cataloging and governance. For The Frontier,
we elected to build `depot` borrowing from some of these best practices, while
also catering to the unique needs and workflows of our lab. While `prospectors` are 
dedicated, modular data curation pipelines, and `stagecoach` acts as a data 
staging workhorse, ferrying data back and forth between folders and the lab's 
datalake, `depot`'s main function is to keep track of `prospector` outputs,
creating visibility into the data curation process. To do this, `depot` 
assumes that a `prospector` has produced one or more datasets suitable for 
reuse by others in the lab. `depot` then uses `datalad` to begin the process of
version control specifically for datasets — dataset registration. After this, `depot` employs the 
`frictionless` data package specification to create a data package for the dataset — 
this tool intended to aid in creating and maintaining metadata about the dataset, 
such as its name, description, and schema. `depot` then uses `datalad` one last 
time to push this data package in a central location (the `gold_mine/02_prospects` 
directory), documenting the action, and providing it to researchers and other tools in the lab.

[^1]: A Prospect is a dataset that has undergone some level of curation and is considered useful for exploration and analysis, but has not yet been formally governed, validated, or certified by the Treasury.
